analysis.one_liner: Requires corporations, unions, super PACs, and tax-exempt groups to disclose election spending and top donors quickly.
analysis.headline: Introduced in March 2026 with 46 Senate Democrats and independents signed on, the bill was referred to the Rules Committee the same day and has sat there since with no hearing, no vote, and no Republican cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require any corporation, labor union, super PAC, or tax-exempt "social welfare" group that spends more than $10,000 to influence a federal election to report that spending to the Federal Election Commission within 24 hours, and to name everyone who gave $10,000 or more. Political ads would have to identify their top funders on screen or on air. It would also extend the existing ban on foreign money to online ads and to state ballot-measure campaigns, make it a federal crime carrying up to five years in prison to set up a shell company to hide foreign money, and — for the first time — require disclosure for ads about federal judicial nominees, an area where spending is currently unreported.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters, who would be able to see who is paying for the political ads they watch and read, and enforcement agencies, which would get new tools to trace foreign money and shell-company spending. Candidates targeted by untraceable spending and federal judicial nominees' confirmation fights would also become more transparent.

how_it_helps.text: Covered organizations — corporations, labor unions, 501(c) tax-exempt groups, and super PACs — that spend more than $10,000 on campaign-related activity must file a report with the FEC within 24 hours, under penalty of perjury, listing anyone who paid them $10,000 or more and every disbursement over $1,000.

The "Stand By Every Ad" title requires political ads in audio, video, and digital formats to carry an on-message disclaimer — for a corporation, its chief executive — plus a list of the organization's top five funders for video ads and top two for audio ads.

The bill extends the ban on foreign-national spending to paid digital and web-based ads and to ballot initiatives and referenda, and makes it a crime, punishable by up to five years in prison, to establish a corporation or entity with the intent to conceal foreign money in elections.

Spending to support or oppose federal judicial nominations — hundreds of millions of dollars from nonprofits that do not disclose donors over the past decade, per the bill's findings — would become subject to the same 24-hour disclosure rules, because such spending currently falls outside federal election law entirely.

The Comptroller General would have to study and report to Congress after each four-year election cycle on the incidence of illicit foreign money in federal elections, including whether it targeted particular communities.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations, labor unions, super PACs, and tax-exempt organizations that spend money to influence elections would bear new compliance and reporting duties, and large online platforms and ad networks would have to handle the expanded ad-disclaimer requirements. Wealthy donors and companies that currently fund political activity through groups that do not name them would lose that anonymity.

drawbacks.text: The reporting duty falls on every covered organization, including labor unions and grassroots advocacy groups, not only on corporate spenders; any covered organization crossing the $10,000 spending threshold must file within 24 hours and identify its $10,000-plus funders.

The bill includes an exemption so donors facing serious threats, harassment, or reprisals can stay unnamed, but the bill's own text excludes mere social ostracism, negative commentary, or criticism from qualifying — a line critics of disclosure laws consider too narrow.

The expanded disclaimers apply to very short digital and video ads, which the bill handles by allowing adapted disclaimers, hover-over text, or a website link rather than a full on-screen funder list — a compromise that still imposes production burdens on small advertisers.

The bill's own findings acknowledge the strongest good-faith objection: opponents argue disclosure requirements chill lawful participation in politics, while the bill cites the Supreme Court's statements in Buckley v. Valeo and Citizens United that disclosure is the least restrictive tool for curbing campaign corruption.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — voters being able to see who pays for the ads aimed at them — is modest to administer and squarely within what the courts have repeatedly upheld as constitutional. The main costs are compliance burdens that fall broadly on unions and advocacy groups as well as corporations, and some donor-exposure risk that the bill mitigates but does not eliminate with its threat exemption. On balance the transparency gains outweigh the compliance costs, though the foreign-money and ballot-measure provisions would face immediate court challenges.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee on the day it was introduced and has taken no further step — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — with the Congress still in session.

narrative.text: Senator Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the bill on March 4, 2026, with 48 other Democratic and independent senators joining as original sponsors.
It has 46 cosponsors: 44 of the 45 Senate Democrats and both independents; no Republican has signed on.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Rules and Administration on the day of introduction, and the public action history shows no further action since.
Republicans hold a 55–45 majority in the Senate, so a bill with no Republican cosponsor has no realistic path to the floor in this Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the groups that spend on elections without naming their funders — corporations, super PACs, and 501(c) social-welfare organizations — are better off, because the rules that let them spend untraceably remain untouched.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Undisclosed campaign spenders keep the status quo

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the 46 cosponsors is a Senate Democrat or an independent who caucuses with them, and no Republican has signed on in a Senate where Republicans hold 55 of 100 seats.

industries.industry: Dark money groups and 501(c)(4) social-welfare organizations
industries.note: These groups spent an estimated $1.05 billion in the 2020 cycle without naming donors, and the bill would force 24-hour disclosure of their election spending and their $10,000-plus funders. Their interest in keeping funders hidden runs directly against voters' interest in knowing who pays for the ads they see.

Corporate treasuries and super PACs would lose the ability to fund election activity anonymously and would face perjury-backed reporting within 24 hours of crossing $10,000 in spending. Their benefit from secrecy comes at the public's cost of not knowing who is behind campaign messages.

The bill closes loopholes that let foreign money reach digital ads and ballot-measure campaigns, and creates a five-year prison penalty for using shell entities to conceal foreign contributions. The FEC found a consultant solicited a $2 million foreign contribution routed through a company and two 501(c)(4) groups, per the bill's findings.

Unions are covered organizations under the bill and would face the same 24-hour reporting and funder-disclosure duties as corporate spenders — a burden unions have historically resisted, even though the transparency standard applies symmetrically to their corporate adversaries.

industries.industry: Large online platforms and digital ad networks
industries.note: Platforms with 50 million or more monthly U.S. users would be pulled into the foreign-money ban and have to carry expanded disclaimers, including top-funder lists or adapted hover-over disclaimers on short ads — a real compliance cost, but one tied directly to the voter-facing benefit.

analysis.trajectory: With the Congress in session until January 2027, the realistic path is that the bill never gets a committee vote: it has no Republican cosponsor in a 55–45 Republican Senate, and campaign-finance bills of this kind would also need 60 votes to overcome a Senate filibuster even if leaders chose to schedule one. Its most likely end is sitting in the Rules Committee until the Congress expires, as prior DISCLOSE Act versions have.
